payload.headline: Microsoft slips 1.97% to 498.3, nearing support; still a hold before January report

summary.thesis: Microsoft's sales and profit margins are getting better, but cash flow fell as spending rose, so the stock is fairly priced only against its own past and expensive on cash flow.
summary.decision: Hold for the long term and add only in the 486.0–491.22 support zone; no swing trade until price reaches that zone.

payload.happening: Microsoft closed at 498.3, down 1.97% on the day. It sits below its flat 20-day (524.96) and 50-day (520.06) averages and just above the 486.0–491.22 support zone, a price area where buyers have stepped in 8 times. News reported that CEO Satya Nadella called the Outlook outage a 'perfect storm', and Nvidia's newsroom reported a wider Azure-to-Windows computing deal with Nvidia; the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
payload.business: Some things change the business itself. Sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier in the latest quarter, a little faster than 18.3% two quarters ago. The operating margin, the share of sales left as profit from operations, rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. The weak spot is cash. Free cash flow (cash left after paying for operations and investment) fell to 60.0B from 78.0B over the trailing year, and the filings show each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year against 51¢ three years ago. That means heavy spending on capacity is not paying back yet. The balance sheet is not at risk: Microsoft holds 29.0B more cash than debt, and liquidity is 64.5B. Other things change only sentiment or governance. The Outlook outage is a reputation issue unless customers leave over it, and nothing in DATA shows that. The Nvidia deal could add demand later, but DATA has no figures for it yet. The reported request that 60K employees quit is unconfirmed and is about how the company is run. It is not shown to affect revenue. Analysts are still raising forecasts: next-year earnings per share (EPS) moved up 2.2% in 30 days to 24.2.

worth.text: There are two ways to value the stock here, and they disagree sharply. A cash-flow model (DCF: today's value of future free cash flow, discounted at 10.1% a year) starts from the trailing 60.0B. It gives 178.92 to 284.38, with 215.82 in the middle. To justify 498.3 on that model, free cash flow would need to start growing at about 40.6% a year. Even 30% starting growth only reaches 340.19. The second method compares today's price-to-sales ratio with Microsoft's own past five years, and it gives 475.73 to 592.92, with 535.43 in the middle. The current price-to-sales of 10.7 sits at the 38th percentile of its own five-year range. The gap between the methods comes from one input: the cash-flow model is anchored to free cash flow that just fell because of spending. On earnings, the stock trades at 26.0 times trailing EPS and 20.6 times next year's estimate. Against peers it looks expensive, at 10.7 times sales compared with a peer median of 3.6. If the operating margin fell to 35%, the cash-flow value would drop to 176.73. My fair-value range is the lower half of the own-history band, because the spending has not yet shown up as cash.
worth.key_assumption: The spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash, so next-year earnings (estimate 24.2) are the right basis for value, not today's cash flow.

bull: Growth is speeding up a little: quarterly sales grew 18.8% from a year earlier, against 18.3% two quarters ago.
Profitability is improving: the operating margin rose to 47.1% from 46.27%.
Analysts keep raising next-year EPS (up 2.2% in 30 days to 24.2), which puts the stock at 20.6 times next year's earnings against 26.0 trailing.
bear: Free cash flow fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and each invested dollar now earns 30¢ a year against 51¢ three years ago.
At 10.7 times sales, the stock costs far more than the peer median of 3.6 without faster growth.
The price implies free cash flow starting to grow at 40.6% a year, while the cash-flow model's middle value is 215.82.

levels.what: Today's close, inside the 475.73–535.43 fair range. There is no reason to sell, but not enough discount for new money.
Top of the strongest support zone (486.0–491.22, 8 touches), close to the 475.73 own-history low. Add here.
Middle of the own-history range. Above it the stock is not cheap even against its own past, and the case for trimming grows toward 592.92.

longterm.why: The business is improving, but two of the three valuation measures lean expensive because free cash flow fell. Today's drop moved the price closer to the add zone but did not reach it.

swing.why: Price is in a range and below the flat 20-day and 50-day averages, with resistance (a price area where selling has capped rallies) close above at 504.96–512.76. The setup becomes valid only on a test of support: entry at 491.22, stop at 480.69, first target at 504.96.

decision.timing: The 2027-02-19 options price a 13.3% move, and that expiry covers the 2027-01-27 report, so new long-term money waits for that report's free cash flow figure unless price first reaches 486.0–491.22.

change_mind: Upgrade to add or buy if the 2027-01-27 report shows trailing free cash flow back toward 78.0B while the operating margin stays at or above 47.1%.
Downgrade from hold to wait if price closes below 472.2, the bottom of the second support zone, which breaks the range.
Turn more cautious if the next-year EPS estimate falls back below 23.68, its level 30 days ago, which would undo the recent upward revisions.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: still a hold. The 1.97% drop to 498.3 moved price toward the 486.0–491.22 add zone without reaching it, and none of today's reported news changes the 60.0B free cash flow problem.
payload.label: Research, not advice.
